body.p: This valuable study compares orthogonal approaches for detecting RNA chemical modifications and provides a helpful framework for improving the reliability of RNA modification identification by direct RNA sequencing. The evidence supporting the technical benchmarking claims is solid, with multiple complementary controls, including in vitro-transcribed RNA, chemical inhibition of METTL3, and orthogonal m6A mapping. However, claims regarding relative method accuracy and cell-type- and isoform-specific biological differences remain less well supported due to limited biological replication and validation.

[Editors' note: this version has been assessed by the Reviewing Editor without further input from the original reviewers. The authors have addressed the comments raised in the previous round of review.]

The authors have substantially strengthened the manuscript in response to my comments. In particular, they have improved the treatment of non-canonical calls, added further illustrative examples at the level of individual RNA variants, repeated pathway enrichment using an appropriate expression-matched background, assessed treatment-associated cell viability, and moderated several biological claims. The revised manuscript is now most compelling as a technical benchmarking and best-practice resource for high-confidence prediction of a common RNA chemical modification from nanopore direct RNA sequencing.

The matched-input comparison of two methods, use of unmodified RNA controls, and inhibitor treatment are important strengths. Together, these experiments provide solid support for the central conclusion that careful filtering and appropriate controls can substantially reduce likely false-positive calls and yield a reproducible set of high-confidence predictions. The added analyses also provide useful illustrations of the capacity of long-read sequencing to assign predictions to individual RNA variants, although they do not establish broad superiority over the short-read comparison method.

The revised manuscript has improved substantially. The authors have addressed the main concerns raised during the previous round by introducing an IVT-based calibration framework, evaluating background calls across probability thresholds, examining basecalling mismatches, and replacing "stoichiometry" with the more appropriate term "predicted modification proportion." The expanded discussion of non-DRACH predictions is also useful and appropriately balanced. Overall, the study now provides a valuable practical framework for Dorado-based RNA modification analysis.
The following is the authors’ response to the previous reviews.

disp-quote.p: The authors have substantially strengthened the manuscript in response to my comments. In particular, they have improved the treatment of non-canonical calls, added further illustrative examples at the level of individual RNA variants, repeated pathway enrichment using an appropriate expression-matched background, assessed treatment-associated cell viability, and moderated several biological claims. The revised manuscript is now most compelling as a technical benchmarking and best-practice resource for high-confidence prediction of a common RNA chemical modification from nanopore direct RNA sequencing.

The matched-input comparison of two methods, use of unmodified RNA controls, and inhibitor treatment are important strengths. Together, these experiments provide solid support for the central conclusion that careful filtering and appropriate controls can substantially reduce likely false-positive calls and yield a reproducible set of high-confidence predictions. The added analyses also provide useful illustrations of the capacity of long-read sequencing to assign predictions to individual RNA variants, although they do not establish broad superiority over the short-read comparison method.

A few claims remain insufficiently supported. First, the discussion of non-DRACH sites should cite Cancer mutations rewire the RNA methylation specificity of METTL3-METTL14 (Science Advances, DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.ads4750). In particular, Figure 3C of that study shows that the normal METTL3-METTL14 enzyme retains measurable activity on non-DRACH substrates; this provides a useful precedent for describing the inhibitor-sensitive GGAUU calls as plausible candidates rather than treating non-DRACH calls, especially those detected only by GLORI, as presumptively artefactual. The revised manuscript appropriately notes technical and biological explanations for non-canonical calls and identifies the GGAUU sites as candidates requiring further validation, but this additional context would improve interpretation.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for reminding us of this interesting publication. We have included the citation and adjusted our discussion accordingly (lines 576-579).

disp-quote.p: Second, the comparison between Dorado and GLORI remains overinterpreted. The matched-input design and inhibitor perturbation are important strengths, but the current analysis does not establish that sites detected only by GLORI are false positives or that Dorado is a reference standard. This would require, for example, direct comparison of inhibitor responsiveness among GLORI-only and shared sites, while accounting for coverage, conversion efficiency, and other method-specific biases; therefore, phrases such as "GLORI exhibits reduced specificity," "largely spurious," and "validated by an orthogonal approach" are not fully supported by the data presented.

body.p: Thank you for this comment. We agree that our original language potentially overinterpreted the GLORI-Dorado comparison. In our GLORI dataset, the relatively high gene-level non-conversion rate (>5%) particularly limits interpretation of low-proportion sites. Although this background has little effect at high m6A/A proportions, it can substantially affect calls in the 10-20% range. Consistent with this limitation, GLORI-only sites were predominantly low-stoichiometry and more often occurred outside DRACH motifs, whereas shared sites were enriched at higher predicted m6 A/A proportions. GLORI coverage was similar between categories, and all sites analyzed were STM2457-responsive. However, residual non-conversion may disproportionately affect low-fraction calls. Thus, our findings do not establish that GLORI-only sites are false positives but instead indicate unresolved method-specific differences. We have adjusted the section accordingly (lines 327-382) and added two additional subplots in Fig. S21 (lines 1193-1202 contain the new figure legends).

disp-quote.p: Similarly, the thresholding approach should not be described as "unbiased." The analysis is useful and empirically informed, but it relies on selected parameters, a manually specified penalty, and predetermined decision criteria. Describing the procedure as "data-driven" or "empirically calibrated against matched unmodified RNA controls" would more accurately convey both its value and its limitations.

body.p: Thank you for this comment. We agree that this language should be used carefully. To our knowledge, we have already refined the relevant wording in the current revised version.

disp-quote.p: The additional RNA-variant examples are helpful, but they demonstrate an advantage of long-read data rather than broadly proving that Dorado "outperforms" GLORI for RNA-variant-level quantification. A more accurate formulation would be: "Direct RNA sequencing provides RNA-variant-resolved predictions that are not readily assignable using short-read GLORI data, as illustrated at several loci."

body.p: We have revised the wording to emphasize that DRS enables RNA-variant-resolved predictions that are not readily assignable using short-read GLORI data (lines 384-385 and 404-406).

disp-quote.p: Finally, the authors now acknowledge that the functional significance of cell-type differences remains unresolved, but the abstract still presents the results as evidence of "finely tuned" regulation, and the discussion links them to neuronal function. The data provide solid evidence for differences in predicted modification proportions between cell types, but the evidence is incomplete for claims about functional consequences; these statements should therefore be framed as context or hypotheses for future study rather than as inferences from the present experiments.

body.p: Thank you for this comment. In the revised manuscript, we do not describe the observed cell-type differences as evidence of “finely tuned” regulation or infer functional consequences for neuronal function. Any potential relevance is framed only as context for future investigation. We refer to lines 43-46 and 602-606, where we describe our observations about increased m6A/A site ratios in HD10.6 cells compared to NHDFs.

disp-quote.p: The revised manuscript has improved substantially. The authors have addressed the main concerns raised during the previous round by introducing an IVT-based calibration framework, evaluating background calls across probability thresholds, examining base calling mismatches, and replacing "stoichiometry" with the more appropriate term "predicted modification proportion." The expanded discussion of non-DRACH predictions is also useful and appropriately balanced. Overall, the study now provides a valuable practical framework for Dorado-based RNA modification analysis.
I have only a few remaining comments, all of which should be addressable through clarification and minor textual revisions.

(1) The comparison between NHDF and HD10.6 cells does not appear to include independent biological replicates. The observed differences in predicted m6A/A proportions should therefore be presented as differences between the two datasets rather than as general cell-type-specific effects. The interpretation is already cautious in the Discussion, but similar wording should be used in the Abstract, Results heading, and title if applicable.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion and agree that the wording should avoid overinterpretation. We consider the title appropriate, as the manuscript reports differences in predicted m6 A proportions between fibroblast and neuronal datasets. However, to ensure greater precision, we revised the relevant sentence in the Abstract (lines 43-46) and two Results section headings (lines 130-131 and 408-409).

disp-quote.p: (2) The direction of the comparison in Figure 3D should be clarified. The percentages represent the fraction of GLORI sites that is also detected by Dorado. Thus, the analysis shows that Dorado increasingly recovers high-proportion GLORI sites. It does not directly demonstrate that high-proportion Dorado predictions are increasingly validated by GLORI. The text should reflect this distinction, and the figure should clearly identify which circle represents each method.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this clarification. We revised the text in lines 367-369 to clarify that Dorado increasingly recovers high-proportion GLORI sites, and we adjusted Fig. 3D to improve clarity.

disp-quote.p: (3) The ratio of calls detected in IVT relative to biological samples is a useful empirical measure of background, but it is not formally a false-positive rate because the true status and testability of every site are not known. A term such as "IVT-to-sample call ratio" or "empirical background-call ratio" would be more precise and would not alter the main conclusion regarding the value of stringent filtering.

body.p: The reviewer’s point is well taken, and we have replaced the use of false-positive with ‘background signal’ throughout the manuscript when dealing with our approach and results. We have however retained the use of false-positive as a term when directly quoting from other published studies (regardless of whether they used this term correctly).

disp-quote.p: (4) The description of the change-point framework still contains the placeholder "at least X-fold more signal." The actual enrichment threshold should be provided. The authors should also ensure that a log2 ratio threshold of 1.5 is not described as 1.5-fold enrichment, since these values are not equivalent.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for catching this. We have corrected the sentence on lines 739-740 to note that the fold enrichment is 1.5-fold which equates to a log2 ratio threshold of ~0.585.

disp-quote.p: These are relatively minor issues. The authors have responded constructively to the previous reviews, and I do not consider further experimental work necessary.

(1) Add the Science Advances reference, DOI: 10.1126/sciadv. ads4750, to the discussion of non-DRACH sites and use it to contextualize inhibitor-sensitive GGAUU sites as plausible candidates requiring independent validation.

(2) Revise language implying that GLORI-only sites are false positives, that GLORI has reduced specificity, or that Dorado serves as the validating reference method; instead, describe the observed agreement and acknowledge unresolved method-specific differences.
(3) If feasible, compare inhibitor responsiveness directly among shared and GLORI-only sites, reporting coverage and conversion-related quality measures for those categories.
(4) Replace "unbiased" thresholding language with "data-driven" or "empirically calibrated against matched unmodified RNA controls."
(5) Revise broad "outperforms" language about RNA-variant-level quantification to specify that long-read sequencing enables predictions at individual RNA variants in the illustrated examples.
(6) Remove or further qualify statements that infer finely tuned regulation or neuronal functional effects from differences in predicted modification proportions alone.

body.p: We have addressed these recommendations as described above.
